transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-08
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood SE); Amir Khan (Cortex Labs CTO), Sofia Ruiz (Head of ML), Ben Carter (Eng Manager)

Summary:
Redwood-led migration/demo focused on parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together APIs to Redwood API. Covered endpoint mapping, function calling differences, streaming, embeddings, token accounting and cost tradeoffs, security (VPC/KMS/SOC2), and next steps for a pilot.

Topics:
- API parity and example mappings (completions/chat/streaming)
- Function/tool calling differences and best practices
- Embeddings migration and vector store compatibility
- Cost/latency tradeoffs and Dedicated vs Hosted
- Security: VPC, KMS, SOC2, audit logs
- POC/benchmark plan and artifacts to share

Action items (captured): see metadata

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Jordan from Redwood, with Priya and Carlos. How's everyone doing at Cortex?
[00:07] Amir Khan: Good thanks, Jordan. Busy but good. Sofia and Ben are here on my side.
[00:11] Sofia Ruiz: Hi. Excited to see how this will line up with our current OpenAI setup.
[00:15] Jordan Lee: Great. Quick agenda: we're going to walk through parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to the Redwood API, show examples for chat/completions, function calling, embeddings, then talk about costs, dedicated options and security. Priya will demo the console and Optimize suggestions.
[00:28] Priya Nair: Hi all. I'll jump in with the API mappings first — sorry if audio is a bit rough on my end.
[00:34] Ben Carter: No worries.
[00:36] Priya Nair: So at a high level, Redwood exposes a unified endpoints for generation, chat and embeddings. If you're currently calling OpenAI's chat.completions or anthropic's responses endpoints, the mapping is straightforward. Example: OpenAI's chat.create -> Redwood /v1/chat, same request/response pattern, we support messages array, role, and streaming via SSE or websockets.
[00:52] Amir Khan: How about model names? We have a lot of internal plumbing that switches on model string and behavior.
[00:57] Priya Nair: Good question. We provide a model catalog with aliases for common upstream models. For example, openai-gpt4 -> redwood-gpt4-compat, anthropic-claude2 -> redwood-claude-compat. We also add compatibility flags for max_tokens, stop sequences, temperature, etc. You can pin specific model versions in the config.
[01:14] Carlos Mendes: Small caveat — sometimes the tokenizer differences mean exact token counts vary a bit between vendors, so the parity mapping spreadsheet (we'll share) has heuristics for prompt truncation and token budgeting.
[01:26] Sofia Ruiz: That's important — we bill and limit per token on our side so we need accurate estimates.
[01:31] Priya Nair: Totally. We'll include an example conversion script snippets in Python and Node that normalize prompts and estimate tokens using Redwood's tokenizer.
[01:41] Jordan Lee: Ok let's demo a live migration example — we have a sample OpenAI chat call and the Redwood equivalent. Priya, you can share your screen.
[01:49] Priya Nair: Sharing. Alright, here's an OpenAI chat request — messages with system/user/assistant, function call request. On Redwood it's the same messages array, and we support function calling via the tools schema. The main difference is our tooling supports stronger typing for tool outputs and a boolean 'return_partial' flag for streaming chunk handling.
[02:07] Ben Carter: Function call behavior — does Redwood auto-execute if the model returns a function call or do we control that in our client?
[02:14] Priya Nair: You control it. The model can return a function call suggestion and you choose to execute. We also have an option to auto-invoke with sandboxed exec in Private deployments but for hosted we recommend explicit execution.
[02:27] Amir Khan: That matches our current flow. How about Together — they have different streaming semantics, we use them for low-latency stuff.
[02:34] Carlos Mendes: Together's streaming is chunked and sometimes out-of-order; Redwood normalizes streaming into an ordered event stream and you can opt into token-level events. Latency-wise, Redwood's runtime is optimized for continuous batching so in many cases we match or beat Together in tail latency, but it depends on model and deployment (hosted vs dedicated).
[02:53] Sofia Ruiz: Do you have numbers? Even ballparks are helpful.
[02:57] Carlos Mendes: For example workloads we saw median p99 reduction from 600ms to ~420ms on the same model when using Redwood Dedicated with optimized kernels. But that depends on sequence lengths and batching. We'll include benchmark templates.
[03:12] Priya Nair: On embeddings, the API looks like OpenAI's embeddings endpoint — you pass input text and get vector back. We support cosine and dot product norms and have helpers for common vector stores. Migration is usually a drop-in: same dimensions for compatible models, but if you change quantization or model family there may be small vector drift; we include migration tests to validate semantic parity.
[03:35] Amir Khan: Semantic drift is a concern — we have similarity thresholds baked into our pipeline. How do you surface regressions?
[03:40] Priya Nair: Redwood Optimize has evaluations tied to prompt sets and embedding regression alerts. You can run baseline comparisons and get signal if similarity drops below configured thresholds.
[03:49] Ben Carter: About auth — we use SSO and want to map our roles to fine-grained permissions for who can change routing/pinning.
[03:57] Jordan Lee: We support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning. Role-based access is exposed in the console — you can control model pinning, rollout policies, and who can trigger Dedicated scale changes. For Private deployments we integrate with existing IdPs.
[04:09] Sofia Ruiz: And encryption? Our legal team wants KMS integration.
[04:12] Carlos Mendes: KMS/HSM integrations are supported for Private and Dedicated. For Hosted we offer managed encryption at rest plus bring-your-own-key (BYOK) options for enterprise. Audit logs and session tracing are available and stored per retention policy.
[04:23] Amir Khan: Our compliance team will ask about SOC2 and ISO.
[04:26] Jordan Lee: We're SOC2 Type II and working on ISO; we'll send the security pack. Priya will attach SOC2 docs and the architecture diagram in the follow-up.
[04:36] Priya Nair: I'll drop the security docs and the parity spreadsheet after the call.
[04:40] Amir Khan: Great. Can you talk about token accounting differences — we're worried about cost when moving models.
[04:46] Priya Nair: On token accounting: our APIs report token counts similar to OpenAI but tokenizer differences can shift counts by a few percent. Redwood Console shows per-route token breakdown and cost estimates. For migrations we recommend running a small A/B on a sample prompt set to measure effective cost delta. Our Optimize tool will suggest batching and cache rules to reduce per-token spend.
[05:08] Ben Carter: Do you do prefix caching? We have lots of repeated system prompts.
[05:11] Carlos Mendes: Yes — prefix/KV caching is supported and can reduce token compute significantly. We can suggest cache keys and TTLs via Optimize.
[05:18] Sofia Ruiz: For latency-sensitive features we might need Dedicated. What's the pilot cadence?
[05:22] Jordan Lee: Typical pilot: 2-4 week proof-of-concept. Start hosted for parity mapping and functional checks, then spin up a small Dedicated pool to run performance benchmarks and validate SLOs. We'll provide a benchmark harness.
[05:34] Amir Khan: How much effort to get Dedicated resources?
[05:36] Jordan Lee: We can provision a small dedicated pool within a week for most regions once contract terms are agreed. It depends on region and instance types.
[05:44] Priya Nair: Quick demo of the Console: here are model catalogs, route configs, and rollout controls. You can set routing policies — for example route to hosted for dev, dedicated for prod, with fallback to a cheaper variant.
[05:58] Ben Carter: Can we set percentage rollouts?
[06:00] Priya Nair: Yes — percent-based canaries and A/B. Also you can set auto-fallback if latency or error rates exceed thresholds.
[06:08] Amir Khan: We use a lot of post-processing tools that rely on function call outputs being strongly typed. You mentioned type enforcement?
[06:15] Priya Nair: We have a schema validation layer for tool outputs that can reject/mask or attempt to coerce. For critical paths we recommend explicit schema and tests in the evals.
[06:26] Jordan Lee: Let's show an example migration of one of your current endpoints. Amir, do you have a typical prompt or flow you can share?
[06:31] Amir Khan: Yeah, we have a customer-support summarization flow. It sends last 10 messages, system prompt, then asks for a structured JSON summary.
[06:38] Priya Nair: Perfect — on Redwood you'd use the chat endpoint and request structured output. We support function-like structured outputs or explicit JSON schema extraction. The difference is our parser is more tolerant to slight format drift and we provide a 'strict_schema' flag.
[06:51] Ben Carter: If strict_schema fails, do you return partial and error codes?
[06:55] Priya Nair: You get a structured error event and the raw text, and you can choose to fallback to a looser parse. This is pluggable in the client.
[07:03] Sofia Ruiz: About embeddings again — vector store compatibility: we store raw vectors but also provide export tools to common stores, right?
[07:10] Carlos Mendes: Right — we have connectors for Pinecone, Milvus, FAISS export helpers, and a lightweight shim to replicate vectors. Migration usually involves re-embedding or a hybrid reindex where you keep old vectors for a short window and validate similarity.
[07:23] Amir Khan: Is there support for incremental re-embedding? We can't re-embed millions at once.
[07:28] Priya Nair: Yes, incremental workflows are recommended; we can help with job orchestration and parallelization tips.
[07:36] Ben Carter: Let's talk about rate limits — Together allows very high concurrency. What's Redwood's approach?
[07:41] Jordan Lee: Hosted has rate limits per account but you can request increases; Dedicated gives you reserved throughput and autoscaling policies. We also have burst capacity options for spikey workloads.
[07:52] Amir Khan: For data residency, we need data to stay in EU. Is that doable?
[07:56] Priya Nair: We have region pinning for Hosted and Dedicated. For strict residency we recommend Private deployment or dedicated region-only hosting with contractual controls.
[08:06] Sofia Ruiz: Ok good. Now a quick question from our infra team — how do you handle KV cache under preemptible instances?
[08:12] Carlos Mendes: We shard KV cache and persist checkpoints; for preemptible nodes we replicate hot keys to avoid tail spikes. The runtime will rehydrate KV from local disk or remote store.
[08:22] Ben Carter: Nice.
[08:24] Amir Khan: Are there any notable incompatibilities when switching from Anthropic to Redwood's safety defaults? We have safety tooling bound up in the flow.
[08:33] Priya Nair: We expose safety controls and content filters similar to Anthropic; you can tune thresholds and we provide a classification API for pre-filtering. For regulated use cases we recommend adding a server-side filter and audit logging.
[08:46] Jordan Lee: Quick timeline idea: initial migration mapping + smoke tests (1 week), hosted parity pilot (2 weeks), performance Dedicated run (1-2 weeks). So around 4-5 weeks end-to-end for a minimal pilot.
[08:58] Sofia Ruiz: That seems reasonable. Cost visibility will be a big factor for our CFO.
[09:02] Jordan Lee: We'll include a cost model based on your sample token usage. If you prefer we can run a side-by-side benchmark using your prompt set and return per-token and per-request cost estimates.
[09:12] Amir Khan: Yes please. We'll share the set.
[09:15] Carlos Mendes: We'll need sample prompts, distribution of sequence lengths, and throughput targets.
[09:20] Ben Carter: For the benchmark, can we simulate production traffic patterns?
[09:23] Priya Nair: Absolutely — our benchmark harness supports ramping patterns and tail latency measurement.
[09:28] Amir Khan: Pros/cons of Hosted vs Dedicated for us? We currently run everything in Hosted with OpenAI.
[09:33] Carlos Mendes: Hosted is fastest to get started and lowest engineering lift. Dedicated gives predictable throughput, lower per-token compute cost in many cases, and data isolation. If you have strict SLOs or compliance, Dedicated or Private is preferred.
[09:47] Sofia Ruiz: Any gotchas in rolling back to OpenAI if something fails?
[09:50] Jordan Lee: We recommend a layered rollout: run Redwood in parallel with existing calls, route a small percentage, compare outputs and costs, then increase. We can provide automated fallbacks to the original vendor if regression or latency issues are detected.
[10:03] Ben Carter: That fallback automation — is that handled in your routing layer or do we need to implement ours?
[10:08] Priya Nair: It's in our routing layer; you configure fallbacks per route, with thresholds for latency/error percent.
[10:15] Amir Khan: Ok, any limitations around streaming long documents? We do longform generation.
[10:20] Carlos Mendes: Longform is supported; the runtime handles KV caching and can chunk sequences across multiple tokens. For extremely long contexts we recommend model-specific tuning and you'll probably want Dedicated so kernel selection and memory management are controlled.
[10:34] Jordan Lee: We'll attach the model compatibility matrix — it lists max context lengths per model and recommended quantizations.
[10:40] Sofia Ruiz: Can you show the Optimize suggestions UI?
[10:43] Priya Nair: Sure. Here is Optimize — it shows suggested batch sizes, cache policies, and which routes are high-cost. It can auto-generate a config patch you can apply.
[10:55] Amir Khan: That patch — is it safe to apply to prod?
[10:58] Priya Nair: It's recommended to apply to a canary route first, Optimize supports generating canary configs.
[11:05] Ben Carter: Regarding SDKs, we use the OpenAI node SDK heavily. How hard is it to migrate client code?
[11:11] Priya Nair: We have drop-in SDKs with wrappers that mimic OpenAI surface area — you can swap a single import in many cases. For Anthropic/Together there's small adapter layers. We'll provide migration snippets.
[11:23] Amir Khan: Ok good. Any enterprise contractual requirements around data deletion?
[11:27] Jordan Lee: We support data deletion APIs and per-tenant retention settings. For Private deployments you control retention fully. Hosted enterprise can set retention windows and purging.
[11:36] Sofia Ruiz: Now maybe move to Q/A — Ben has a question about monitoring.
[11:40] Ben Carter: Can we integrate Redwood traces into our existing tracing system?
[11:44] Carlos Mendes: Yes — we emit span events and traces that can be shipped to Datadog/Zipkin/NewRelic. Also the Console shows per-token timelines.
[11:53] Amir Khan: Ok let's recap the immediate next steps.
[11:56] Jordan Lee: Recap: 1) We'll share the parity mapping sheet and migration guide (Priya). 2) Jordan will share pricing and pilot options. 3) Cortex to share prompt set and token distribution. 4) Schedule POC kickoff.
[12:11] Sofia Ruiz: Sounds good. Any other blockers?
[12:13] Amir Khan: Legal will want security docs — please include SOC2 and KMS specifics.
[12:17] Priya Nair: We'll attach the security pack and a short architecture doc.
[12:21] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts.
[12:24] Amir Khan: Appreciate it. Looking forward.
[12:26] Jordan Lee: End call.

Notes on transcription: some words may be auto-corrected (e.g. Redwood sometimes shown as Redboard) and speaker labels are best-effort.
